title: States of Matter and the Particle Model

content.text: States of Matter and the Particle Model
Introduction

Everything around you, from the air you breathe to the chair you sit on, is made up of incredibly tiny particles. These particles are in constant motion, and the way they are arranged and move determines whether a substance exists as a solid, a liquid, or a gas. Understanding the particle model of matter is one of the most fundamental ideas in physics, because it allows us to explain a huge range of everyday observations, from why ice melts to why you can smell perfume from across a room.
In this lesson, we will explore the three states of matter in detail, examine the evidence that particles really do exist and move, and understand how substances change from one state to another.
Key Concepts
The Three States of Matter
All matter exists in one of three common states: solid, liquid, or gas. Each state has distinct properties that arise from the arrangement, spacing, and motion of its particles.
Solids

In a solid, particles are packed closely together in a regular, ordered arrangement. They are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction between them. However, the particles are not completely still. They vibrate back and forth about their fixed positions. The higher the temperature, the more vigorously they vibrate.
Key properties of solids:
Fixed shape: because particles are locked in position
Fixed volume: because particles are tightly packed
High density: because particles are close together
Incompressible: because there is very little space between particles
Do not flow: because particles cannot move past each other
Liquids

In a liquid, particles are still close together but they are no longer in a regular arrangement. The forces between particles are weaker than in a solid, which means the particles can slide past one another. They move randomly within the body of the liquid.
Key properties of liquids:
No fixed shape: takes the shape of its container
Fixed volume: particles are still close together
Moderate to high density: only slightly less dense than the solid form in most cases
Nearly incompressible: very small gaps between particles
Can flow: particles can move past each other
Gases

In a gas, particles are widely spaced and move rapidly in random directions. The forces between particles are negligible except during brief collisions. Gas particles travel in straight lines until they collide with another particle or with the walls of their container.
Key properties of gases:
No fixed shape: fills the entire container
No fixed volume: expands to fill any space available
Very low density: particles are far apart
Easily compressed: large gaps between particles can be reduced
Flows easily: particles move freely in all directions
The Kinetic Particle Model
The kinetic particle model (sometimes called the kinetic theory of matter) is based on several key ideas:
All matter is made up of very small particles (atoms, molecules, or ions).
These particles are in constant motion. The higher the temperature, the faster they move on average.
There are forces of attraction between particles. These forces are strongest in solids and weakest in gases.
The average kinetic energy of the particles is directly related to the temperature of the substance.

This model is extremely powerful because it allows us to explain macroscopic properties (things we can observe and measure, like pressure and temperature) in terms of microscopic behaviour (what individual particles are doing).
Brownian Motion: Evidence for Particles
In 1827, the botanist Robert Brown observed that pollen grains suspended in water moved in a jerky, random, zigzag pattern. This random motion is now called Brownian motion.

The explanation is straightforward using the particle model: the pollen grains are being bombarded from all sides by water molecules that are far too small to see. At any given instant, the bombardment is slightly uneven, with more molecules hitting one side than the other. This causes the visible pollen grain to jerk in a random direction. A moment later, the imbalance is in a different direction, so the grain jerks another way.

Brownian motion can also be observed with smoke particles in air. Under a microscope, tiny smoke particles are seen to move in a random, erratic path because they are being struck by invisible air molecules.
Brownian motion provides strong evidence that:
Particles of matter really do exist
These particles are in constant, random motion
The particles move faster at higher temperatures (Brownian motion becomes more vigorous when the temperature is increased)
Diffusion
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, as a result of their random motion.
Examples of diffusion include:
The smell of cooking spreading through a house
A drop of ink spreading through a beaker of water
Perfume being detected across a room

Diffusion happens because particles are in constant random motion. Although each individual particle moves randomly, the overall effect is a net movement from where there are many particles to where there are few. Eventually, the particles become evenly distributed.
Important facts about diffusion:
Diffusion is faster at higher temperatures, because particles move faster
Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids, because gas particles move more freely and quickly
Diffusion does not occur in solids under normal conditions, because particles are locked in fixed positions
Lighter molecules diffuse faster than heavier ones (at the same temperature), because they move at higher average speeds

A classic demonstration involves placing a piece of cotton wool soaked in hydrochloric acid at one end of a glass tube and a piece soaked in ammonia solution at the other end. A white ring of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube, closer to the hydrochloric acid end. This is because ammonia molecules (
\text{NH}_3
, molecular mass 17) are lighter than hydrogen chloride molecules (
\text{HCl}
, molecular mass 36.5), so the ammonia molecules diffuse faster.
Changes of State
A substance can change from one state to another when energy is added or removed. These changes of state are physical changes, meaning no new substance is formed and the process can be reversed.
The six changes of state are:
Melting
(solid to liquid): Energy is supplied to the solid. Particles vibrate more vigorously until they have enough energy to break free from their fixed positions and move past each other.
Freezing
(liquid to solid): Energy is removed from the liquid. Particles slow down until the forces of attraction lock them into fixed positions.
Boiling
(liquid to gas): Energy is supplied to the liquid. Particles gain enough energy to completely overcome the forces of attraction and escape from the surface and from within the body of the liquid.
Condensation
(gas to liquid): Energy is removed from the gas. Particles slow down enough for the forces of attraction to pull them close together.
Sublimation

(solid directly to gas): Some substances can change directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state. This happens when particles at the surface of the solid gain enough energy to escape directly into the gas phase. Examples include dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) and iodine crystals when gently heated.
Deposition

(gas directly to solid): The reverse of sublimation. Gas particles lose energy and form a solid directly, without passing through the liquid state. An example is frost forming on cold surfaces from water vapour in the air.
Particle Energy During Changes of State
A crucial concept is what happens to the temperature during a change of state. When a substance is melting or boiling, its temperature remains constant even though energy is still being supplied.

Why does this happen? During a change of state, the energy being supplied is used to break or weaken the bonds (forces of attraction) between particles, rather than to increase their kinetic energy. Since temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, the temperature does not change until the change of state is complete.
For example, when ice at 0°C is being heated:
The temperature stays at 0°C while the ice melts
All the energy goes into breaking the bonds that hold the particles in their fixed solid arrangement
Only after all the ice has melted does the temperature of the water begin to rise
Similarly, when water at 100°C is boiling:
The temperature stays at 100°C
All the energy goes into breaking the remaining forces between liquid particles so they can escape as gas
The energy required for boiling is much greater than for melting, because in boiling the particles must completely overcome all attractive forces
Mathematical Relationships
While the states of matter topic is largely conceptual at this level, there are some quantitative relationships worth noting.
The average kinetic energy of particles in a gas is proportional to the absolute temperature (measured in kelvin):
E_k \propto T
This means that if you double the absolute temperature, you double the average kinetic energy of the particles.
The density of a substance relates to the mass and volume:
\rho = \frac{m}{V}
where
\rho
is density in
\text{kg/m}^3
m
is mass in kg, and
V
is volume in
\text{m}^3
Solids typically have the highest density (particles packed tightly), followed by liquids, and then gases (particles widely spaced). For example, the density of water in its three states:
Ice: approximately
917 \text{ kg/m}^3
Liquid water: approximately
1000 \text{ kg/m}^3
Steam: approximately
0.6 \text{ kg/m}^3
Notice that ice is actually less dense than liquid water. This is an unusual property of water that has important consequences, which we will explore in later lessons.
Worked Examples
Worked Example 1: Explaining Diffusion
Problem:
A student opens a bottle of perfume at the front of a classroom. After a few minutes, students at the back of the room can smell it. Explain this observation using the particle model.
Solution:

The perfume is a volatile liquid that evaporates, releasing perfume molecules into the air. These molecules have kinetic energy and move in random directions. They collide with air molecules and bounce off in new random directions. Although the motion of each molecule is random, there is a net movement of perfume molecules from where their concentration is high (near the bottle) to where their concentration is low (the back of the room). This process is diffusion. Over time, the perfume molecules spread throughout the room, allowing students at the back to detect the scent.
Worked Example 2: Brownian Motion
Problem:

Smoke particles viewed under a microscope are seen to move in a random, jerky path. The same experiment is repeated at a higher temperature, and the motion becomes more vigorous. Explain both observations.
Solution:

The smoke particles are small but much larger than air molecules. They are constantly bombarded by air molecules from all sides. At any instant, the bombardment is slightly unequal, causing a net force in a random direction. This makes the smoke particle move in a jerky, unpredictable way.

At a higher temperature, the air molecules have greater average kinetic energy and move faster. Their collisions with the smoke particles are more forceful, causing the smoke particles to be knocked about more vigorously. This is why the random motion increases at higher temperatures.
Worked Example 3: Heating Curve Analysis
Problem:
A block of ice at
is heated steadily. Describe what happens to the temperature and the particles as the ice is heated until it becomes steam at
Solution:
The ice warms up. Particles vibrate more vigorously in their fixed positions. Temperature rises steadily.
Stage 2 (at $0°C$):
The ice melts. Temperature remains constant at
. Energy is used to break the bonds holding particles in their rigid structure. Particles begin to move past each other.
The liquid water warms up. Particles move faster and more randomly. Temperature rises steadily.
Stage 4 (at $100°C$):
The water boils. Temperature remains constant at
. Energy is used to completely overcome the forces of attraction between particles. Particles escape from the liquid as gas.
The steam heats up. Gas particles move even faster. Temperature rises steadily.

Solution:

Common Misconceptions
Misconception 1: "Particles expand when heated"

Particles themselves do not get bigger when heated. What actually happens is that particles move faster and vibrate more vigorously, causing them to push further apart from each other. The spaces between particles increase, not the size of the particles.
Misconception 2: "There is air between particles"

The spaces between particles in a gas are empty. There is nothing between the particles. In a vacuum, there are no particles at all. Air itself is made of particles (nitrogen and oxygen molecules), so it cannot exist between other particles.
Misconception 3: "Particles stop moving in solids"
Particles in a solid are always vibrating about their fixed positions. They never completely stop moving. Particles would only stop if the temperature were absolute zero (
or
0 \text{ K}
), which can never actually be reached.
Misconception 4: "Boiling and evaporation are the same thing"

Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a specific temperature (the boiling point) and requires a continuous supply of energy. Evaporation occurs only at the surface of a liquid, can happen at any temperature, and results in cooling. We will explore this distinction in detail in a later lesson.
Misconception 5: "Gases are weightless"

Gases have mass, just like solids and liquids. A balloon filled with air is slightly heavier than an empty (deflated) balloon. Gas particles are simply more spread out, giving gases a much lower density.
Misconception 6: "During a change of state, particles gain or lose energy"

More precisely, during a change of state, the substance gains or loses energy, but the kinetic energy of the particles does not change (temperature stays constant). The energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles, which is potential energy, not kinetic energy.

Practice Problems
Problem 1:
Describe the arrangement, motion, and spacing of particles in a solid, a liquid, and a gas. State the relative strength of the forces between particles in each state.
Problem 2:
Explain why a gas can be compressed easily but a liquid cannot be compressed easily. Use the particle model in your answer.
Problem 3:
A student places a drop of food colouring into a beaker of cold water and another drop into a beaker of hot water. Explain why the colour spreads faster in the hot water, using the particle model.
Problem 4:

State the name of the process by which naphthalene (mothballs) gradually gets smaller when left in a wardrobe, even though the temperature is well below its melting point. Explain this process using the particle model.
Problem 5:
A substance is heated steadily. Its temperature rises from
to
, then stays constant at
for several minutes while heating continues, and then begins to rise again. State what is happening at
and explain why the temperature remains constant during this period.
Problem 6:
Calculate how many times denser iron (
\rho = 7870 \text{ kg/m}^3
) is than air (
\rho = 1.2 \text{ kg/m}^3
). Explain this difference using the particle model.
Problem 7:
Describe and explain why smoke particles in a Brownian motion demonstration move more vigorously when a light source (which heats the air) is brought close to the smoke cell.
Problem 8:
Compare the rate of diffusion in gases and liquids. Explain why diffusion occurs more quickly in gases than in liquids.
Summary
All matter is made of tiny particles that are in constant motion.
In
solids
, particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.
In
liquids
, particles are close together but can slide past each other in a random arrangement.
In
gases
, particles are widely spaced and move rapidly in random directions.
Brownian motion
(the random, jerky movement of visible particles suspended in a fluid) provides evidence that invisible molecules exist and are in constant motion.
Diffusion
is the net movement of particles from high concentration to low concentration, caused by random particle motion.
Substances change state when energy is added (melting, boiling, sublimation) or removed (freezing, condensation, deposition).
During a
change of state
, the temperature remains constant because the energy supplied is used to break or form bonds between particles, not to change their kinetic energy.
The
kinetic particle model
explains macroscopic observations (like pressure, temperature, and density) in terms of the behaviour of individual particles.
Answer Key
Solid:
particles in a regular, closely packed pattern; vibrate about fixed positions; strong forces between particles.
Liquid:
particles close together but in a random arrangement; slide past each other; moderate forces.
Gas:
particles far apart with large spaces between them; move rapidly in random directions; very weak forces (negligible except during collisions). — (explanation with physics reasoning)
Gas particles are far apart with large spaces between them
, so when a force is applied the particles can be pushed closer together, reducing the volume easily.
Liquid particles are already very close together
with very little space between them, so there is almost no room for the particles to move closer, making liquids nearly incompressible. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
The colour spreads faster in the hot water.

At a higher temperature, the water molecules have greater average kinetic energy and move faster. They collide with the food colouring particles more forcefully and more frequently, causing the dye particles to diffuse more rapidly through the water. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
The process is sublimation.

Naphthalene changes directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state. At the surface of the solid, some particles have enough kinetic energy to overcome the attractive forces holding them in the solid structure and escape directly into the gas phase. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
The substance is melting (changing state from solid to liquid) at $80°C$.

The temperature remains constant because the energy being supplied is used to break the bonds between particles (increasing their potential energy), not to increase their kinetic energy. Since temperature depends on average kinetic energy, it stays the same until all the solid has melted. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
$7870 \div 1.2 = 6558$ times denser.

Iron is approximately 6600 times denser than air. In iron (a solid metal), particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement with very small gaps. In air (a gas), particles are widely spaced with large gaps between them, resulting in much less mass per unit volume. — (calculation)
The air molecules gain kinetic energy from the heat source and move faster.

They strike the smoke particles with greater force and more frequently, causing the smoke particles to be knocked about more vigorously. The increased Brownian motion is direct evidence that higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy of the air molecules. — (explanation with physics reasoning)
Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids.

In gases, particles move freely and rapidly in random directions with few obstructions, covering large distances between collisions. In liquids, although particles are closer together, they are constantly colliding with neighbouring particles, which slows their net movement. Gas particles also have higher average speeds than liquid particles at the same temperature due to weaker intermolecular forces. — (comparison)
